claim: Transition-state (TS) theory has provided the theoretical framework to explain the enormous rate accelerations of chemical reactions by enzymes.
source: Transition-state (TS) theory has provided the theoretical framework to explain the enormous rate accelerations of chemical reactions by enzymes.
evidence: This is a statement about the established role of TS theory in explaining enzyme catalysis, supported by citation to Truhlar, 2015 in the full text.

claim: Proteins display large ensembles of conformations.
source: Given that proteins display large ensembles of conformations, unique TSs would pose a huge entropic bottleneck for enzyme catalysis.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in protein science, referenced in the context of the manuscript's argument.

claim: Unique transition states would pose a huge entropic bottleneck for enzyme catalysis.
source: Given that proteins display large ensembles of conformations, unique TSs would pose a huge entropic bottleneck for enzyme catalysis.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the ensemble nature of proteins and thermodynamic principles.

claim: A structurally wide set of energetically equivalent configurations lie along the reaction coordinate for the phosphoryl-transfer step in adenylate kinase.
source: We find a structurally wide set of energetically equivalent configurations that lie along the reaction coordinate and hence a broad transition-state ensemble (TSE).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the QM/MM calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: A broad transition-state ensemble exists for the phosphoryl-transfer step in adenylate kinase.
source: We find a structurally wide set of energetically equivalent configurations that lie along the reaction coordinate and hence a broad transition-state ensemble (TSE).
evidence: This is directly stated as a finding from the computational studies.

claim: A conformationally delocalized ensemble, including asymmetric TSs, is rooted in the macroscopic nature of the enzyme.
source: A conformationally delocalized ensemble, including asymmetric TSs, is rooted in the macroscopic nature of the enzyme.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Enzyme kinetics experiments confirm the decrease of the entropy of activation predicted from a wide TSE.
source: The computational results are buttressed by enzyme kinetics experiments that confirm the decrease of the entropy of activation predicted from such wide TSE.
evidence: This refers to experimental measurements of activation parameters presented in Figure 5.

claim: Enzymatic rate acceleration is due to the enzymes' much higher affinity to the TS relative to its substrates.
source: A wealth of research has led to the general notion that enzymatic rate acceleration is due to the enzymes' much higher affinity to the TS relative to its substrates.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in enzymology, supported by citations to Lienhard, 1973 and Schramm, 2007.

claim: High affinities measured for transition-state analogs relative to substrates support the idea of TS stabilization.
source: This idea has been supported experimentally by the high affinities measured for transition-state analogs (TSA) relative to substrates, leading to the design of TSA as high-affine enzyme inhibitors (Lienhard, 1973; Schramm, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental evidence cited in the literature (Lienhard, 1973; Schramm, 2007).

claim: The uncatalyzed phosphoryl-transfer reaction would take about 7000 years.
source: This chemical step would take about 7000 years without the enzyme (Stockbridge and Wolfenden, 2009) compared to >5000 s−1 with the enzyme (Kerns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Stockbridge and Wolfenden, 2009.

claim: The enzyme-catalyzed phosphoryl-transfer reaction in adenylate kinase occurs at a rate >5000 s−1.
source: This chemical step would take about 7000 years without the enzyme (Stockbridge and Wolfenden, 2009) compared to >5000 s−1 with the enzyme (Kerns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: Adenylate kinase catalyzes the reversible conversion of two ADP molecules into ATP and AMP.
source: Adk is an extensively studied phosphotransferase that catalyzes the reversible, roughly isoenergetic conversion of two ADP molecules into ATP and AMP (Figure 1A, B), thereby maintaining the cellular concentrations of these nucleotides (Dzeja and Terzic, 2009).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about Adk function, supported by citation and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The conversion of two ADP molecules into ATP and AMP by adenylate kinase is roughly isoenergetic.
source: Adk is an extensively studied phosphotransferase that catalyzes the reversible, roughly isoenergetic conversion of two ADP molecules into ATP and AMP (Figure 1A, B), thereby maintaining the cellular concentrations of these nucleotides (Dzeja and Terzic, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Dzeja and Terzic, 2009.

claim: Adenylate kinase maintains cellular concentrations of adenine nucleotides.
source: Adk is an extensively studied phosphotransferase that catalyzes the reversible, roughly isoenergetic conversion of two ADP molecules into ATP and AMP (Figure 1A, B), thereby maintaining the cellular concentrations of these nucleotides (Dzeja and Terzic, 2009).
evidence: This is a known biological function of Adk, cited from Dzeja and Terzic, 2009.

claim: Lid-closing positions the two substrates and the active-site residues for efficient chemistry in adenylate kinase.
source: Lid-closing positions the two substrates and the active-site residues for efficient chemistry (i.e., P-transfer) and prohibits the alternative, energetically favorable reaction of phosphoryl hydrolysis (Kerns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: Lid-closing prohibits the alternative, energetically favorable reaction of phosphoryl hydrolysis in adenylate kinase.
source: Lid-closing positions the two substrates and the active-site residues for efficient chemistry (i.e., P-transfer) and prohibits the alternative, energetically favorable reaction of phosphoryl hydrolysis (Kerns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: Lid-opening, not P-transfer, is the rate-limiting step in the adenylate kinase catalytic cycle.
source: Lid-opening, essential for product release, and not P-transfer is the rate-limiting step in the catalytic cycle and Mg2+ accelerates both steps (Kerns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: Mg2+ accelerates both lid-opening and P-transfer steps in adenylate kinase.
source: Lid-opening, essential for product release, and not P-transfer is the rate-limiting step in the catalytic cycle and Mg2+ accelerates both steps (Kerns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: The free-energy activation barrier for the fully charged nucleotide state is ΔfG‡ of 13 ± 0.9 kcal/mol in the presence of Mg2+.
source: The results reveal a much smaller free energy of activation for the fully charged nucleotide state (ΔfG‡ of 13 ± 0.9 kcal/mol) relative to monoprotonated state (ΔfG‡ of 23 ± 0.9 kcal/mol) (Table 1)
evidence: This is a direct result from the QM/MM calculations presented in Table 1.

claim: The free-energy activation barrier for the monoprotonated nucleotide state is ΔfG‡ of 23 ± 0.9 kcal/mol in the presence of Mg2+.
source: The results reveal a much smaller free energy of activation for the fully charged nucleotide state (ΔfG‡ of 13 ± 0.9 kcal/mol) relative to monoprotonated state (ΔfG‡ of 23 ± 0.9 kcal/mol) (Table 1)
evidence: This is a direct result from the QM/MM calculations presented in Table 1.

claim: The fully charged nucleotide state is the most reactive enzyme configuration for adenylate kinase.
source: The results reveal a much smaller free energy of activation for the fully charged nucleotide state (ΔfG‡ of 13 ± 0.9 kcal/mol) relative to monoprotonated state (ΔfG‡ of 23 ± 0.9 kcal/mol) (Table 1); hence, we conclude that this is the most reactive enzyme configuration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational data comparing activation barriers.

claim: The free-energy activation barrier without Mg2+ is ΔfG‡ of 34 ± 1.6 kcal/mol for the monoprotonated nucleotide.
source: When the calculations were repeated in the absence of Mg2+ (with the nucleotide monoprotonated, since the fully charged nucleotide state prohibited the reaction), a large increase in the free-energy activation barrier was observed relative to the Mg2+-bound system (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, ΔfG‡ of 34 ± 1.6 kcal/mol)
evidence: This is a direct result from the QM/MM calculations.

claim: Mg2+ provides an overall acceleration of >105-fold for the phosphoryl-transfer reaction in adenylate kinase.
source: We note that only a lower limit for the overall acceleration by Mg2+ (>105-fold) could be estimated from published results (Kerns et al., 2015), since the P-transfer was too fast to be measured experimentally in the presence of Mg2+.
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: A contraction of the active site is observed while passing through the TSE in adenylate kinase.
source: For Adk, a contraction of the active site is observed while passing through the TSE, as captured by the decrease in the distance between acceptor and leaving group during the transition (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations and shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: In the absence of Mg2+, the acceptor and donor need to be within 4 Å for the reaction to occur.
source: In the absence of Mg2+, the acceptor and donor need to be within 4 Å for the reaction to occur (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the presence of Mg2+, an acceptor–donor distance of 4.5 Å is sufficient for the reaction to occur.
source: whereas in the presence of Mg2+ an acceptor–donor distance of 4.5 Å is sufficient (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The TSE changes from tight/synchronous without Mg2+ into loose with Mg2+.
source: The TSE changes from tight/synchronous without Mg2+ (meaning high bond-order for both bonds between transferring phosphate to the leaving group and the attacking nucleophile) into loose with Mg2+ (lower bond-order for these two bonds; Figures 2 and 3; Lai and Cui, 2020a; Lai and Cui, 2020b; Roston et al., 2018; Roston and Cui, 2016).
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations shown in Figures 2 and 3, and is consistent with definitions from cited literature.

claim: The enzyme operates with a wide TSE in the presence of Mg2+.
source: In other words, the enzyme seems to operate with a wide TSE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational observations of multiple conformations with equal free energy.

claim: Without Mg2+, fewer conformations comprise the TSE.
source: In contrast, without Mg2+ fewer conformations seem to comprise the TSE.
evidence: This is observed from the computational simulations comparing reactions with and without Mg2+.

claim: The difference in position of the transferring phosphate along the reaction coordinate within the TSE is about 1 Å with Mg2+.
source: The difference in position of the transferring phosphate along the reaction coordinate within the TSE (about 1 Å with Mg2+; Figure 1c, Figure 2 and Figure 3b)
evidence: This is measured from the computational simulations and shown in the figures.

claim: The TSE contains many highly asymmetric conformations.
source: The difference in position of the transferring phosphate along the reaction coordinate within the TSE (about 1 Å with Mg2+; Figure 1c, Figure 2 and Figure 3b) implies that the TSE contains many highly asymmetric conformations
evidence: This is inferred from the computational data showing the range of phosphate positions.

claim: The asymmetry in the TSE is tied with nonplanar configurations of the transferring phosphate.
source: This asymmetry is logically tied with nonplanar configurations of the transferring phosphate (Figure 3D and Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the computational results in Figure 3D and Table 1.

claim: Mg2+ enables the donor and acceptor phosphates to come close enough to react.
source: It enables the donor and acceptor phosphates to come close enough to react, thus achieving a reactive conformation.
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations comparing reactions with and without Mg2+.

claim: In the absence of Mg2+, a proton must bridge the terminal phosphates to prevent strong electrostatic repulsion.
source: In the absence of Mg2+, a proton must bridge the terminal phosphates to prevent the strong electrostatic repulsion between the two nucleotides.
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations without Mg2+.

claim: Mg2+ stabilizes the charge of the transferring phosphate and thereby lowers the enthalpic barrier.
source: In addition, Mg2+ stabilizes the charge of the transferring phosphate and thereby lowering the enthalpic barrier.
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations and charge analysis.

claim: The presence of a cation results in a wide TSE.
source: Most interestingly, the presence of a cation seems to result in a wide TSE.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing computational results with and without Mg2+.

claim: R85 arranges the beta-phosphates of the ADPs in the proper position for the reaction to be started.
source: R85 appears to arrange the beta-phosphates of the ADPs in the proper position for the reaction to be started.
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations analyzing the role of active site residues.

claim: R150 and R161 are involved in anchoring ATP and AMP residues in the backward reaction.
source: R150 and R161 are involved in anchoring ATP and AMP residues in the backward reaction.
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations analyzing the role of active site residues.

claim: R36 is near to the alpha-phosphate of AD(M)P along the entire catalytic reaction, stabilizing both the TS and products.
source: R36 is near to the alpha-phosphate of AD(M)P along the entire catalytic reaction, stabilizing both the TS and products.
evidence: This is observed in the QM/MM simulations analyzing the role of active site residues.

claim: The calculated difference in activation barriers with and without Mg from umbrella simulations is about 9.5 kcal/mol.
source: Notably, the calculated difference in activation barriers with and without Mg from these umbrella simulations of about 9.5 kcal/mol is in good agreement with the experimentally determined ones of ≥11 kcal/mol
evidence: This is calculated from the umbrella sampling simulations.

claim: The experimentally determined difference in activation barriers with and without divalent cation is ≥11 kcal/mol.
source: Notably, the calculated difference in activation barriers with and without Mg from these umbrella simulations of about 9.5 kcal/mol is in good agreement with the experimentally determined ones of ≥11 kcal/mol (P-transfer with Mg is >500 s−1 (Kerns et al., 2015) compared to 7.5 × 10−4 s−1 measured here).
evidence: This is determined from experimental kinetics measurements.

claim: P-transfer rate with Mg is >500 s−1.
source: P-transfer with Mg is >500 s−1 (Kerns et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: P-transfer rate without Mg is 7.5 × 10−4 s−1.
source: compared to 7.5 × 10−4 s−1 measured here
evidence: This is measured experimentally in this study.

claim: A delocalized TSE for the fully active enzyme results in a lowering of the entropic barrier for the chemical step.
source: This feature would result in a lowering of the entropic barrier for the chemical step, thereby contributing to the enzyme-catalyzed rate enhancement.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the computational findings.

claim: The divalent cation is predicted to lower the activation entropy.
source: Since the reaction with Mg2+ (fully active enzyme) revealed a more pronounced delocalization than the reaction in its absence, the divalent cation is predicted to lower the activation entropy.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the computational results showing a wider TSE with Mg2+.

claim: The enthalpic contribution to the chemical reaction barrier in the presence of Ca2+ is ΔH‡ of 15.3 ± 0.5 kcal/mol.
source: The resulting Eyring plots for the two experiments (Figure 5A) deliver the enthalpic (ΔH‡ of 15.3 ± 0.5 and 16.7 ± 1 kcal/mol) and entropic (ΔS‡ = −5.7 ± 1.6 and −19.1 ± 3.1 cal/mol/K) contributions to the chemical reaction barrier in the presence and absence of Ca2+, respectively.
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The enthalpic contribution to the chemical reaction barrier in the absence of divalent cation is ΔH‡ of 16.7 ± 1 kcal/mol.
source: The resulting Eyring plots for the two experiments (Figure 5A) deliver the enthalpic (ΔH‡ of 15.3 ± 0.5 and 16.7 ± 1 kcal/mol) and entropic (ΔS‡ = −5.7 ± 1.6 and −19.1 ± 3.1 cal/mol/K) contributions to the chemical reaction barrier in the presence and absence of Ca2+, respectively.
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The entropic contribution to the chemical reaction barrier in the presence of Ca2+ is ΔS‡ = −5.7 ± 1.6 cal/mol/K.
source: The resulting Eyring plots for the two experiments (Figure 5A) deliver the enthalpic (ΔH‡ of 15.3 ± 0.5 and 16.7 ± 1 kcal/mol) and entropic (ΔS‡ = −5.7 ± 1.6 and −19.1 ± 3.1 cal/mol/K) contributions to the chemical reaction barrier in the presence and absence of Ca2+, respectively.
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The entropic contribution to the chemical reaction barrier in the absence of divalent cation is ΔS‡ = −19.1 ± 3.1 cal/mol/K.
source: The resulting Eyring plots for the two experiments (Figure 5A) deliver the enthalpic (ΔH‡ of 15.3 ± 0.5 and 16.7 ± 1 kcal/mol) and entropic (ΔS‡ = −5.7 ± 1.6 and −19.1 ± 3.1 cal/mol/K) contributions to the chemical reaction barrier in the presence and absence of Ca2+, respectively.
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of Ca2+ reduces both enthalpic and entropic barriers considerably.
source: The presence of Ca2+ reduces both barriers considerably.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental measurements comparing reactions with and without Ca2+.

claim: There is a large decrease in the entropic barrier in the presence of a divalent cation.
source: The striking new result, central to this work, is the large decrease in the entropic barrier in the presence of a divalent cation, thereby strongly supporting our key finding of a broader TSE from the QM/MM simulations.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental measurements and supports the computational predictions.

claim: The reaction rate increases with higher pH in the presence of Ca2+.
source: We find that the reaction rate increases with higher pH in the presence of Ca2+, whereas without a metal the opposite trend is observed (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Without a metal, the reaction rate decreases with higher pH.
source: We find that the reaction rate increases with higher pH in the presence of Ca2+, whereas without a metal the opposite trend is observed (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At low pH (pH 5), the P-transfer step becomes rate limiting even with Mg2+.
source: Notably, at low pH (pH 5), the P-transfer step becomes rate limiting even with Mg2+, allowing for an estimate of the rate enhancement of Mg2+ versus Ca2+ of 24-fold.
evidence: This is observed from experimental measurements at different pH values.

claim: The rate enhancement of Mg2+ versus Ca2+ is 24-fold.
source: Notably, at low pH (pH 5), the P-transfer step becomes rate limiting even with Mg2+, allowing for an estimate of the rate enhancement of Mg2+ versus Ca2+ of 24-fold.
evidence: This is estimated from experimental measurements.

claim: Single Arg to Lys mutations show large decreases in the catalytic rate.
source: The large decrease in the catalytic rate for each single Arg to Lys mutation further highlights the notion of a highly choreographed active site for a well-coordinated P-transfer (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is measured experimentally for mutants R36K, R85K, R124K, R150K, and R161K as shown in Table 2.

claim: Full lid-closure results in excellent preorientation of the donor and acceptor groups of the two bound nucleotides.
source: Full lid-closure results in an excellent preorientation of the donor and acceptor groups of the two bound nucleotides and the aiding active-site residues in the enzyme/substrate complex, in agreement with the general view of necessary pre-organization in enzyme catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural and computational analysis.

claim: Enzymes provide a fundamentally different, advantageous way to catalyze chemical reactions compared to the uncatalyzed reaction by employing a broad TSE.
source: Here, we uncover a central new result that provokes a modified TS theory. Enzymes, due to their macromolecular nature, provide a fundamentally different, advantageous way to catalyze these chemical reactions compared to the uncatalyzed reaction by employing a broad TSE.
evidence: This is the central conclusion of the manuscript based on computational and experimental results.

claim: Many different molecular configurations can be accommodated in the TS region with comparable energies via collective motions.
source: Many different molecular configurations can be accommodated in the TS region with comparable energies via collective motions, spanning a 1-Å range along the reaction coordinate for the transferring phosphate that travels a total distance of only 2 Å during the P-transfer.
evidence: This is observed from the QM/MM simulations.

claim: The transferring phosphate travels a total distance of only 2 Å during the P-transfer.
source: Many different molecular configurations can be accommodated in the TS region with comparable energies via collective motions, spanning a 1-Å range along the reaction coordinate for the transferring phosphate that travels a total distance of only 2 Å during the P-transfer.
evidence: This is measured from the QM/MM simulations.

claim: The findings explain why enzymes do not face an entropic bottleneck for catalysis.
source: Our findings explain why enzymes do not face an entropic bottleneck for catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discovery of the wide TSE.

claim: The TSE comprises highly asymmetric conformations due to the asymmetric nature of enzyme active sites.
source: Furthermore, as enzyme active sites are asymmetric in contrast to the symmetric nature of the solvent for uncatalyzed reactions, we find that the TSE comprises also highly asymmetric conformations.
evidence: This is observed from the QM/MM simulations and is a logical consequence of active site structure.

claim: A conformationally spread-out TSE is likely one reason why enzymes are much bigger than a few active-site residues.
source: A conformationally spread-out TSE is likely one reason why enzymes are much bigger than a few active-site residues
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the findings.

claim: Residues remote from the site of chemical action allow for conformational flexibility without the protein unfolding.
source: On the one hand residues remote from the site of the chemical action allow for conformational flexibility without the protein unfolding
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for enzyme size based on the TSE concept.

claim: Remote residues reduce excursions into unproductive conformations.
source: while reducing excursions into unproductive conformations (Otten et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Otten et al., 2020.

claim: The configurations seen in the simulations are along the P-transfer reaction coordinate.
source: The latter mechanism is directly demonstrated here in the TSE, as the configurations seen in the simulations are along the P-transfer reaction coordinate.
evidence: This is observed from the QM/MM simulations.

claim: Nature evolves a conformational step to be rate limiting as the 'price' the enzyme pays for stabilizing the ES complex.
source: We propose that this is the 'price' the enzyme pays for stabilizing the ES complex to enable efficient rate acceleration of the chemical step, and for suppressing detrimental alternate reactions such as phosphate hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for why lid-opening is rate limiting.

claim: Extensive electrostatic interactions of five Arg and one Lys with the phosphoryl groups efficiently accelerate the P-transfer step.
source: These principles have now been directly revealed on an atomic scale for Adk: extensive electrostatic interactions of five Arg and one Lys with the phosphoryl groups to efficiently accelerate the P-transfer step, which then need to be broken for lid-opening to allow product release.
evidence: This is observed from the QM/MM simulations and mutational studies.

claim: The importance of TSE for protein folding has been well documented.
source: The importance of TSE including multiple transition pathways for protein folding (Frauenfelder et al., 2006; Royer, 2008), and more recently for protein conformational transitions within the folded state (Pontiggia et al., 2015; Stiller et al., 2019; Tsai and Nussinov, 2014) has been well documented.
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Protein folding and function is embedded in a unifying energy landscape which is simply altered by ligands and solvent.
source: Consequently, protein folding and function is embedded in a unifying energy landscape which is simply altered by ligands and solvent.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion about protein energy landscapes.

claim: The X-ray structure of Adk in complex with Ap5A coordinated to Zn2+ (2RGX) was used as the starting structure for QM/MM simulations.
source: The starting structures for the simulations were prepared using the X-ray structure of Adk in complex with Ap5A (P1,P5-Di(adenosine-5′) pentaphosphate) and coordinated to Zn2+ (2RGX; Henzler-Wildman et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used.

claim: The QM region was defined as the diphosphate moiety of both ADP molecules, the Mg2+ ion, plus the four coordinating water molecules.
source: For the QM/MM simulations, the QM region was defined as the diphosphate moiety of both ADP molecules, the Mg2+ ion, plus the four coordinating water molecules.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used.

claim: The equilibrated starting structures agree well with the X-ray structures of the enzyme bound to Mg2+/ADP (4CF7).
source: The equilibrated starting structures agree well with the X-ray structures of the enzyme bound to Mg2+/ADP (4CF7; Kerns et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This validates the computational setup by comparison with experimental structures.

claim: Higher-level pure DFT(PBE) free-energy calculations are in excellent agreement with the FEPs obtained from SCC-DFTB calculations.
source: During revision, we tested the accuracy and robustness of our results from our original QM/MM level of theory by employing higher-level pure DFT(PBE) free-energy calculations similar to the approaches used by Ganguly et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 6. The results are in excellent agreement with the FEPs obtained before (Figure 1C, E; Figure 2A, C) thus further supporting the computational results.
evidence: This validates the computational results by using a higher level of theory.

claim: A concerted mechanism is observed with no intermediates for the phosphoryl-transfer in Adk.
source: For Adk, a concerted mechanism is observed with no intermediates (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is observed from the QM/MM simulations shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Umbrella sampling FEPs corroborate the key difference in the range of the TSE.
source: The umbrella sampling FEPs (Figure 4a–d) corroborate the key difference in the range of the TSE.
evidence: This is shown by the umbrella sampling calculations in Figure 4.

claim: The activation free energies are smaller for the umbrella sampling when compared to the multiple steered molecular dynamics (MSMD).
source: Noteworthy, the activation free energies are smaller for the umbrella sampling when compared to the multiple steered molecular dynamics (MSMD).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the results from the two computational methods.

claim: Exponential averaging tends to overestimate free-energy barriers.
source: It is well known that exponential averaging tends to overestimate free-energy barriers, and particularly when they are too high (Park et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Park et al., 2003.

claim: The commitment analysis displays a very shallow change along the reaction coordinate in the presence of Mg2+.
source: A consequent comparative commitment analysis that calculates the probability of reaching either reactants or products displays a very shallow change along the reaction coordinate in the presence of Mg2+, further corroborating a wide TSE for the P-transfer step in the fully active enzyme
evidence: This is shown by the commitment analysis in Figure 4d.

claim: The commitment analysis shows a narrow and steep change in the committors without Mg2+, indicative of a narrower TSE.
source: in stark contrast to a narrow and steep change in the committors indicative of a narrower TSE without Mg2+ (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is shown by the commitment analysis in Figure 4d.

claim: Ca2+ is an appropriate mimic to selectively probe the chemical step in place of Mg2+.
source: The experimental trick of replacing Mg2+ with Ca2+ was used since the chemical step with Mg2+ is too fast to be experimentally measured, and previous studies showed that Ca2+ is an appropriate mimic to selectively probe the chemical step (Kerns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Kerns et al., 2015.

claim: The fully charged nucleotides state was the most reactive in the presence of the metal.
source: These experimental results match the simulation results: the fully charged nucleotides state was the most reactive in the presence of the metal, whereas the monoprotonated state had a much higher free-energy barrier.
evidence: This is concluded from the pH-dependent kinetics experiments matching the computational predictions.

claim: Without metal, only the monoprotonated nucleotides were reactive.
source: In contrast, without metal only the monoprotonated nucleotides were reactive.
evidence: This is concluded from the pH-dependent kinetics experiments matching the computational predictions.
